title: Lesson 15.1 — When to Fine-Tune — and When Not To
intro: This is lesson fifteen point one: when to fine-tune, and when not to. We will follow one engineer at a Nigerian fintech startup, from a two-week deadline to a working decision. By the end you will have a framework for choosing a strategy, instead of reaching for fine-tuning by default.

sections.name: The two-week deadline
narration: This is a growing fintech startup in Lagos.
An engineer has just been handed a pile of customer support messages.
A manager says: we need an AI system that can categorize these in two weeks.
The engineer looks at the pile, then at a blank screen labeled Build AI Model.

sections.name: Don't build from zero

explain.heading: Don't Build From Zero
explain.note: Start with a model that already knows a lot — and specialize it for your job.

narration: The obvious move is to build a model from zero.
That means labeling thousands of examples by hand, renting servers, and watching months flip past on the calendar.
Then everything freezes, because a pre-trained model drops into the scene as a machine that has already done most of the work.
You don't have to teach a model everything from zero.
You can start with a model that already knows a lot, and specialize it for your job.

sections.name: The real question

explain.heading: The Real Question
explain.note: Data · Task similarity · Performance · Time · Compute

narration: Now put two giant buttons on the screen: fine-tune, and don't fine-tune yet.
The engineer reaches toward one, then stops.
Because the decision engineers actually need to make is a different one.
Five factors settle it: your data, how similar your task is, the performance you need, your time, and your compute.

sections.name: A skilled worker

explain.heading: A Skilled Worker, Not a Blank Slate
explain.note: It doesn't start that education over — it specializes what the model already knows.

narration: Think of the pre-trained model as an experienced worker.
This worker has already spent years reading books, articles, messages and documents.
Then we hand the worker a much smaller stack, labeled customer support emails.
A pre-trained model has already learned general patterns from enormous amounts of data.
Fine-tuning doesn't start that education over, it specializes what the model already knows.

sections.name: What fine-tuning changes

explain.heading: What Fine-Tuning Actually Changes
explain.note: It already knew language. Now it specializes in our problem.

narration: So what actually changes inside the model when you fine-tune?
Picture billions of tiny adjustable dials, the parameters and the weights.
During fine-tuning, only relatively small adjustments are made, using task-specific data.
A general language model becomes a customer support specialist.
It already knew language, and now it specializes in our problem.

sections.name: Standing on what exists

explain.heading: Standing on What Already Exists
explain.note: Transfer learning: reuse knowledge learned for one problem on another related problem.

narration: This is standing on what already exists.
Picture a tall building, where the lower floors hold general patterns.
The upper floors adapt to your task, whether that is customer complaints, medical terminology, or financial language.
This is transfer learning.
Reuse knowledge that was learned for one problem when you solve another related problem.

sections.name: The trap

explain.heading: The Trap: A Model That Memorizes
explain.note: The model didn't learn the problem. It learned the examples.

narration: Now for the trap, back to the fintech emails with only three hundred of them labeled.
During training the model becomes increasingly confident, and accuracy reaches ninety-eight percent.
Then completely new emails arrive, and the numbers collapse to sixty percent, then fifty-five.
The model didn't learn the problem.
It learned the examples.
It stuffed individual emails into a filing cabinet, instead of finding the pattern that connects them.

sections.name: Catastrophic forgetting

explain.heading: When Fine-Tuning Goes Too Far
explain.note: Overfitting — and catastrophic forgetting: pre-trained knowledge, damaged.

narration: Fine-tuning can also go too far.
Picture the pre-trained model as a large library, holding years of general knowledge.
Fine-tune it aggressively on a tiny stack of emails, and it starts ripping books off the shelves, replacing them with copies of your three hundred examples.
That is overfitting, and when it damages knowledge the model already had, it is called catastrophic forgetting.
The cause is simple: too much adjustment on too little data.

sections.name: Two roads

explain.heading: Two Roads
explain.note: Two different strategies, with different trade-offs.

narration: So there are two roads.
On the left, feature extraction, where the pre-trained model stays frozen and only a small model on top of it learns.
On the right, fine-tuning, where data enters the model and parts of the model change.
These aren't two versions of the same technique.
They're two different strategies with different trade-offs.

sections.name: The data scale

explain.heading: The Data Scale Changes the Decision
explain.note: How much data you have changes how much of the model you can safely adapt.

narration: The amount of data you have changes which road you take.
With a very small dataset, use feature extraction, and keep the model frozen.
With a medium dataset, use layer-wise fine-tuning, and unlock some of the layers.
With a large dataset, you can fine-tune fully and adapt the whole model.
The amount of data you have changes how much of the model you can safely adapt.

sections.name: The decision board
narration: So here is the engineer's decision board.
Ask about the model: is there a related pre-trained model I can start from?
Ask about the data: how much labeled data do I have, and how different is my task?
Ask about the budget: how much time and compute do I have, and how important is peak performance?
Every answer sends a glowing path toward one of three strategies.

sections.name: The Nigerian fintech case

explain.heading: The Nigerian Fintech Case
explain.note: Data size, task difference, timeline, compute, and performance — all point the same way.

narration: Now let's walk the fintech case through the board.
The constraints are twelve hundred labeled interactions, a two-week timeline, and one GPU.
The requirements are ninety percent accuracy or better, with a related pre-trained language model available.
The data is too small to retrain everything, but large enough to safely unfreeze part of the model.
So the board lands on layer-wise fine-tuning.

sections.name: Red flags

explain.heading: Red Flags
explain.note: Having data doesn't automatically mean you should fine-tune.

narration: Before you commit, watch for the red flags.
Too little data, the wrong pre-trained model, poor-quality labels.
A task that needs knowledge the model doesn't have, or extreme time pressure.
Each one blocks the path toward fine-tuning.
Having data doesn't automatically mean you should fine-tune.
Sometimes the smartest move is to fix the problem before training anything.

sections.name: The final decision

explain.heading: The Final Decision
explain.note: Choose the strategy with the right balance — not the most powerful one.

narration: So we are back to the two buttons.
This time the engineer doesn't reach immediately, because the five decision factors appear around them.
The choice comes only after weighing performance, cost, risk, time, and resources.
Fine-tuning is not the default.
It is one tool in your toolbox, and choosing it is an engineering decision.

sections.name: Summary

explain.heading: Ask Whether — Then How Much
explain.note: Data · Task similarity · Performance · Time · Compute

narration: Look at where we started: a pile of customer emails.
Very little data, and they go through feature extraction with the model frozen.
A medium amount, and they go through layer-wise fine-tuning, unlocking some of the layers.
Plenty of data, and they go through full fine-tuning, adapting every layer.
Above them, the five decision factors stay visible.
So from this point forward, when you see a fine-tuning problem, don't start by asking how to train the model.
Start by asking whether the model should be changed at all, and how much.
